title: Kant's Categorical Imperative
objective: After this level you can apply Kant's categorical imperative, in its universal-law and never-merely-as-a-means forms, to a false promise.
summary: Kant’s categorical imperative rules out a false promise: made universal, promising collapses, and the lender is used merely as a means. Mill said the test counts consequences.

cards.headline: You need a loan, and you’ll only get it by promising to repay. You can’t.
cards.body: Just this once? Kant used exactly this case to show how his test of right and wrong works.

cards.headline: “If you want” versus “you must”
cards.body: Kant separated two kinds of command. A hypothetical imperative says an action is good for some purpose: if you want the end, take the means. A categorical imperative declares an action necessary in itself, with no reference to any purpose. Moral duty, Kant held, speaks in the second voice. It doesn’t care what you happen to want.

cards.headline: Test one: could everyone do it?
cards.body: In Thomas Abbott’s translation: “Act only on that maxim whereby thou canst at the same time will that it should become a universal law.” Try the false promise. Whenever I need money, I’ll promise to repay, knowing I can’t. Make that a universal law and promising itself becomes impossible. Nobody would believe a promise; people would laugh at such statements as vain pretences.

cards.headline: Test two: people aren’t tools
cards.body: Another form: treat humanity, in yourself or anyone else, always as an end and never merely as a means. The word “merely” matters. You may use a taxi driver to get home, as long as you respect him as a person with his own ends. The false promiser uses the lender merely as a tool, in a way the lender could never agree to.

cards.headline: Mill’s complaint
cards.body: Level 46’s Mill pounced on test one. When Kant derives actual duties, Mill wrote, he fails “almost grotesquely” to show any real contradiction. “All he shows is that the consequences of their universal adoption would be such as no one would choose to incur.” Kantians reply that the contradiction is real: a lying promise needs a practice of trust that its own universal version abolishes.

cards.headline: Kant’s Categorical Imperative: the big picture
learned: Hypothetical: if you want X. Categorical: you must
Universal law: could everyone act on your maxim?
A false promise makes promising impossible
Mill: Kant’s test secretly counts consequences

questions.prompt: Match each part of Kant’s ethics with what it says.

pairs.right: If you want the end, take the means

questions.explanation: A hypothetical imperative says if you want the end, take the means. A categorical one declares an action necessary in itself. Test one asks could everyone do it; test two says people aren’t tools.

questions.prompt: In Kant’s argument, why does a universal law of false promising defeat itself?

options.label: Lenders would charge much higher interest to cover their losses
options.rationale: That’s a consequence, not Kant’s contradiction.

options.label: No one would believe promises, so none could work
It would break the law of the land

questions.explanation: If everyone made lying promises, promising would become impossible, since no one would believe one.

questions.prompt: Mill, Level 46’s utilitarian, said Kant’s universal-law test really shows what?

options.label: That lying is sometimes a duty
That universal adoption would bring consequences nobody would choose
That Kant quietly agreed with Bentham’s measures of pleasure
options.rationale: Mill’s point is about Kant’s test, not Bentham’s list.

questions.explanation: Mill argued Kant found no real contradiction, only consequences of universal adoption that no one would choose to incur.
